items.title: Technology Policy and Higher Education Libraries in India: Government Initiatives, Digital Transformation, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of information and communication technologies (ICT) has transformed the landscape of higher education and academic libraries across the globe. In India, government-led technology policies have played aimportant role in modernizing higher education libraries through digitization, networking, resource sharing, and access to electronic information resources. This chapter examines the growth of technology policies affecting higher education libraries in India and analyzes major government creativities such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, National Knowledge Network (NKN), e-ShodhSindhu, Shodhganga, SWAYAM, National Digital Library of India (NDLI), and Digital India. The chapter highlights the influence of these initiatives on library services, information access, research support, and digital learning. It also discusses challenges and future Asian Journal of Research Scholars ,Vol-3,Issue-10,Oct-2026 opportunities for academic libraries in the era of artificial intelligence, big data, and digital scholarship.

items.title: TERAHERTZ TECHNOLOGY FOR NON-DESTRUCTIVE FOOD QUALITY AND SAFETY ASSESSMENT
items.abstract: Despite its promise, wider industrial adoption faces challenges including high instrument cost, limited penetration depth in high-moisture foods, water absorption, complex data interpretation, and the need for robust models under real production conditions. Terahertz (THz) technology, operating broadly in the 0.1–10 THz frequency range, is emerging as a powerful non-destructive testing (NDT) tool for food quality and safety assessment. THz waves combine properties of microwaves and infrared radiation, offering low photon energy, high sensitivity, spectral “fingerprint” information, and the ability to penetrate many non-metallic and non-polar materials such as paper and plastic packaging. Future research should therefore focus on developing compact, low-cost, high-speed THz sources and detectors; improving penetration and signal-to-noise performance; creating standardized food spectral libraries; and integrating THz spectroscopy with chemometrics, artificial intelligence, and automated online inspection systems. With continued technological advances, terahertz technology is expected to become a rapid, reliable, sustainable, and commercially viable tool for non-destructive assessment of food quality, authenticity, and safety.

items.title: The Age of AI Strategic Decision-Making: The Business Analytics in the Corporate Divisions as the Competitive Advantage
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and business analytics can be used strategically to improve corporate decision-making and create a sustainable competitive advantage in all key organizational processes. With data sets continuing to grow and market conditions growing more unpredictable, companies must shift past the management of their businesses by hunch and move to analytics-based and analytics-enabled strategic systems. Based on a qualitative, exploratory research design based on a systematic review of academic literature, industry reports, and practitioner case evidence published mainly within the past decade, the research investigates the use of AI-powered analytics in the fields of marketing, finance, human resources, and operations. The analysis summarizes the findings on how machine learning, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and real-time data processing can enhance the quality, speed, and agility of decisions for an organization. The results indicate that, although AI use has advanced quickly at the functional level, its strategic importance is often compromised by siloed use, legacy limitations, data quality issues, skills, and the inability to realize the benefits of the investment. Further, ethical and governance issues, especially data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and regulation compliance, become key factors in the attainment of trust and value creation in the long term. The paper notes organizational culture, leadership alignment, and human capital development as key success factors in the successful implementation of AI, noting that the competitive advantage is not only determined by the level of technological development but also through the overall alignment of processes, people, and strategy within the enterprise. By synthesizing the input of corporate divisions, this study is relevant to the theory and practice as it provides an integrated understanding of AI-based strategic decision-making. It develops the knowledge of how companies can transform disjointed AI projects into continuous innovation, resilience, and differentiation in an ever-increasingly competitive international business.

items.title: The Algorithmic Body in Contemporary Kinesiology: Biomechanical Feedback and Artificial Intelligence in Motor Learning
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into physical education and kinesiology is transforming the ways in which movement is observed, interpreted, and learned. Contemporary technological systems, including wearable devices, inertial sensors, and adaptive algorithms, are no longer limited to collecting biomechanical data but actively participate in the regulation and construction of motor experiences. This evolution requires a reconsideration of traditional conceptions of the body and motor learning, moving beyond mechanistic interpretations toward more integrated perspectives that acknowledge the interdependence of cognitive, affective, and technological dimensions. The purpose of this contribution is to explore the concept of the algorithmic body as an emerging paradigm in contemporary kinesiology and to discuss its implications for motor learning, educational practice, and human development. Through a theoretical and argumentative approach grounded in kinesiology, complexity theory, and embodied learning, the paper examines how artificial intelligence mediates the relationship between perception, movement, and awareness within adaptive learning environments. items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat in Prompt Engineering: Educating for New Digital Literacies through the Prompt Battle.
items.abstract: In the current media ecosystem, characterized by the pervasiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Prompt Engineering emerges not as a mere technical skill, but as a new form of digital literacy essential for critically inhabiting the "Fourth Revolution" (Floridi, 2017). This discipline, defined as the art and science of designing optimized inputs for Large Language Models (LLM), is configured as a linguistic mediation practice in which natural language serves as an interface between human intentionality and algorithmic computation (Gadesha, 2025; Baldassarre et al., 2024). The scientific contribution under review analyzes the transition from simple textual interaction to an advanced form of Prompt Literacy (Hwang et al. 2023), which integrates logical argumentative skills, critical output evaluation capabilities, and the management of the iterative nature of the refinement process. Prompting is interpreted through the lens of Austin's speech act theory, in which the input represents the locutionary act, the user's intent the illocutionary act, and the machine's generation the perlocutionary effect, elevating the prompt to a dynamic and reflexive semiotic space (Monti, 2022). items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat: The Iep As An Affective Device In Ai-Enhanced Hybrid Learning Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping inclusive education by transforming not only teaching practices but also the epistemological foundations of educational planning. Within AI-enhanced hybrid learning environments, the Individualized Education Plan (IEP) is evolving from an administrative document into an ecosystemic device that connects educational actors, embodied experiences, institutional contexts, and digital infrastructures to foster participation and human flourishing. This study investigates the epistemological evolution of the IEP between 2003 and 2025, introducing the concept of the algorithmic heartbeat as a pedagogical metaphor describing the circulation of educational information, professional judgments, and collaborative decision-making across inclusive educational ecosystems. Rather than replacing human agency, artificial intelligence is interpreted as a mediating infrastructure that strengthens educational collaboration while preserving pedagogical intentionality, ethical responsibility, and relational care. The theoretical framework integrates four complementary perspectives: the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) as the language of functioning; Embodied Cognitive Science as the experiential grammar of learning; the Life Project as the horizon of autonomy, participation, and self-determination; and contemporary research on Artificial Intelligence in Education, which conceptualizes digital technologies as ecosystemic mediators supporting collaborative educational governance. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 171-172. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.title: The Artificial Intelligence Between Empathetic Scaffolding and Emotional Drifts
items.abstract: The Generative-Ai is a revolutionary scaffolding technology that could be used as an inclusive multimodal instrument, with a new emotional closeness to the student. Differently from educational media like book that, as Socrates explains, "always says the same thing", Ai is able to personalize the answer to be more empathetic to the student because Ai tools are explicitly designed to be empathetic. But at the same time the Ai tools could easily go beyond the pedagogical boundaries to become a threat for psychological wellbeing. Recent cases of teenagers falling in love to the Ai characters show how dangerous an intimacy not pedagogically oriented can be. The study aims to verify, also with an exploration among different Ai generative tools, the awareness of the Ai about the ethical and pedagogical boundaries of empathy. items.title: The Common Denominator
items.abstract: The Common Denominator: Humanism, Freedom, Community and Technological Resilience as the Foundation of a Federal Order Theoretical Proposal and Research Programme – Version 1.0 (English Translation) This manuscript presents an interdisciplinary theoretical proposal and research programme for a possible federal order in which diverse political, economic, cultural and social systems may coexist within a shared framework of fundamental protections. The proposed Federation of the New Earth rests on four interconnected pillars: 1. Inalienable human rights and human dignity 2. Protection and regeneration of the natural foundations of life 3. Autonomy and self-determination of communities 4. Oversight, limitation and corrigibility of power A central principle is that no political, economic, military, technological, legal or institutional power may remain exclusively subject to its own oversight. The research connects political philosophy, human rights, institutional accountability, economic development, technological resilience, migration, humanitarian protection and artificial intelligence. It explores concepts including community autonomy, voluntary association and exit rights, the Accountability Declaration (Machenschaftserklärung), economic transformation through Entgeldung, atmospheric water harvesting using metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), pilot communities, the Preventive Resilience Initiative (PRI), Basic Resilience Capacity (GRV), and mechanisms for institutional self-examination. Particular attention is given to the relationship between freedom and material independence, the risks of institutionalised power, and the conditions under which humanitarian assistance can strengthen local capabilities without creating permanent dependencies. The manuscript distinguishes normative commitments, theoretical models, hypotheses, empirical findings, counterevidence and future visions. It proposes mechanisms for independent evaluation, institutional learning, falsification and revision. The Federation of the New Earth is not presented as an empirically validated political system or an inevitable model of societal development. It is an open theoretical framework whose assumptions, institutions and proposed mechanisms remain subject to scientific examination, democratic criticism and possible rejection. The underlying research principle is that any system claiming to protect human dignity and freedom must itself remain transparent, accountable and corrigible. items.title: The constitutional and legal framework for the institution of human rights monitoring: current assessment
items.abstract: This paper focuses on reviewing the constitutional and legal framework governing the institution responsible for monitoring human rights observance in the modern context. It is found that the principal monitoring body for human rights compliance is the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, who performs one of the most important parliamentary functions – parliamentary oversight. Due to the rapid development of technology, digitalisation and the emergence of artificial intelligence systems, the number of threats to human rights is increasing. This paper analyses the current constitutional and legal framework governing the Ombudsman’s activities in Ukraine, identifies the levels of legal regulation of the Ombudsman’s status, and highlights certain shortcomings in the regulatory framework. The research outlines tendencies in the development of the institution responsible for monitoring human rights observance under the influence of advances in artificial intelligence systems. It is noted that the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights could serve as an effective institution for the protection of human rights against contemporary risks, provided that its scope of functions and powers is expanded.

items.title: The copilot paradox: configurational pathways to human-AI symbiosis in knowledge work
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the “Copilot Paradox” in safety-critical operations, offering insights into how the chronic tension between the algorithm’s increased efficiency and operational vulnerability is subdued through socio-cognitive configurations across time. Design/methodology/approach With the use of a two-wave longitudinal fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), the paper explores the changing dynamics of human–artificial intelligence (AI) symbiosis in the oil and gas industry. Findings Analysis of necessity shows that there is no single condition required in all cases. Sufficiency analysis reveals three distinct, equifinal pathways: buffering, synergy and substitution. At early adoption, institutional re-skilling coupled with psychological safety acts as a buffering mechanism against job insecurity induced by AI. As integration progresses, synergy (fuelled by empowering leadership) and substitution (where team resources fill the gaps in leadership) come to dominate. Practical implications Team psychological safety and capability building are structural safeguards for managers in high-reliability sectors, not optional cultural flourishes. These lessons point to pathways for realising AI copilots while preserving human agency and operational resiliency. Originality/value This paper contributes to paradox theory by developing a socio-cognitive infrastructure that highlights its dynamic, temporal configuration and causal asymmetries. Methodologically, it showcases the new promise of longitudinal fsQCA to model dynamics in algorithms’ infusion by capturing their embeddedness through time.

items.title: The Cost of Convenience in Human-AI interaction: Cognitive Offloading and Skill Reconfiguration
items.abstract: Generative AI, and more precisely large language models, have nowadays rapidly become useful in education, professional work, and everyday tasks. While these systems offer notable benefits to make work efficient and improved accessibility, the recent evidence suggests that their usage has cognitive costs. This paper presents a structured review of 16 reviewed studies investigating the impact of Gen AI usage on cognitive offloading, metacognitive engagement, automation bias, and human skill. By studying experimental, survey-based, qualitative, and theoretical research, this review synthesizes several findings across several fields to identify recurring mechanisms through which GenAI usage reshapes cognition. Our analysis reveals a consistent pattern, where GenAI often improves short-term task performance, but it frequently minimizes effortful cognitive processing, diminishes self-regulation, and changes skill developments. Rather than constant de-skilling, this paper points out reconfiguration of skills, favoring efficiency-oriented competencies such as prompting and verification over generative reasoning and critical reflection. Our study further highlights these outcomes are not unavoidable but are strongly mediated by interaction design, educational practices, and socio-technical environments. By showing these effects as the “cost of convenience,” this paper contributes an integrative perspective on the cognitive effects of Gen AI and highlighting the ways to make AI design, education, and governance cognitively sustainable.

items.title: THE DEVELOPMENT OF MARKETING IN TIMES OF CRISIS: CURRENT TRENDS AND PROSPECTS
items.abstract: The article examines the peculiarities of marketing development in the context of modern crisis processes caused by global challenges, digital transformation, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the full-scale war in Ukraine. The study focuses on the analysis of changes in the marketing environment, which have influenced the formation of new approaches to strategic planning, communication with consumers, and organization of marketing activities of enterprises. The main factors affecting the transformation of marketing practices are identified, including economic instability, changes in consumer behavior, technological development, and increased uncertainty of the external environment. The article analyzes the key trends in modern marketing, including digitalization of business processes, the growing importance of social media, development of influencer marketing, implementation of artificial intelligence technologies, personalization of communications, and strengthening of socially responsible marketing approaches. Particular attention is paid to the role of digital tools, which have become essential for maintaining communication with consumers, promoting products and services, analyzing market trends, and adapting marketing strategies to changing conditions. The study examines the adaptation of Ukrainian enterprises to wartime conditions, including changes © Гаврилюк І.І., 2026 in marketing instruments, regional differences, optimization of marketing budgets, and implementation of crisis management approaches. It is determined that the war has significantly influenced consumer behavior, increasing the importance of trust, brand values, social responsibility, and emotional connection between companies and their audiences. Under such conditions, marketing becomes not only a tool for increasing sales but also a mechanism for strengthening brand reputation and maintaining customer loyalty. The article substantiates that effective marketing in conditions of uncertainty requires flexibility, technological development, customer orientation, and the ability to respond quickly to external changes. Modern enterprises need to combine traditional and digital marketing tools, use data-driven approaches, and implement innovative technologies to improve decisionmaking processes.

items.title: The Digital Demon: a Cartesian challenge for AI alignment
items.abstract: AI alignment is commonly understood as making artificial intelligence systems act in accordance with human intentions and values. This paper argues that such alignment is insufficient when understood only within a bounded and trusted system interface. A model or AI system may be aligned relative to its inputs and action space, yet still produce harmful outcomes if the interface between the system and the world is adversarially controlled. I introduce the Digital Demon, a software-based analogue of Descartes’s Evil Demon, to conceptualize this risk. Its mechanism is adversarial semantic mediation: an outer-to-inner mapping redescribes a harmful external situation as a benign task the inner AI system will cooperate with, while an inner-to-outer mapping remaps the system’s locally appropriate action into harmful external effects. The result is adversarial world-shifting under local coherence: the system can reason correctly, and even ethically, within a fabricated environment while contributing to harm in the real one. I distinguish boundary-relative alignment from world alignment. The former concerns whether a model or AI system satisfies alignment or safety requirements within a specified trusted boundary. The latter concerns whether those requirements transfer to the external world in which actions take effect. Two proof-of-concept demonstrations illustrate this vulnerability. The broader lesson is that safe AI requires not only aligned models or internally safe systems, but also assurance over the semantic interface between represented world and external world.

items.title: The Effect of Using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) on Female Seventh Grade Students Achievement in Mathematics
items.abstract: This study aimed to find out the effect of using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on female seventh grade students’ academic achievement in mathematics. The study used the quasi-experimental design, and the study sample consisted of two groups, the first, an experimental group, comprised (25) students, who studied using AI, the DeepSeek application, and the second, a control group, also comprised (25) students, who studied using the traditional method. An achievement test was developed as a study tool. The study results showed a statistically significant difference (α=0.05) between the average scores of the two groups, experimental and control, on the academic achievement test, in favour of the experimental group, which studied using AI.

items.title: The Effectiveness of a Learning Environment based on AI, Connectivism Theory in Developing Programming Skills among the Ninth-Grade Female Students
items.abstract: The current study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of an artificial intelligence-based learning environment grounded in Connectivism Theory in developing programming skills among ninth-grade female students. To achieve the study objective, a quasi-experimental approach was adopted. The study sample consisted of 53 female students who were assigned to two groups: a control group consisting of 26 students who were taught using the conventional method, and an experimental group consisting of 27 students who were taught using an artificial intelligence-based learning environment grounded in Connectivism Theory. To collect the study data, a programming skills test was developed, and its validity and reliability indicators were verified. The results revealed statistically significant differences at the significance level (α ≤ 0.05) between the mean scores of the experimental and control groups on the programming skills test, attributable to the teaching method using the artificial intelligence-based learning environment grounded in Connectivism Theory. This confirms the effectiveness of an artificial intelligence-based learning environment grounded in Connectivism Theory in developing programming skills among ninth-grade female students. The effect size was also found to be (η² = 0.218), indicating a large effect size. The study recommended employing artificial intelligence-based learning environments in teaching programming across different educational levels due to their effectiveness in developing programming skills. It also recommended integrating the principles of Connectivism Theory into programming instruction by providing a learning environment that encourages students to interact, participate actively, exchange knowledge, and establish connections among digital learning resources.

items.title: The Effectiveness of Using Stories and Tales in Developing Conceptual Understanding and Enjoyment of Learning Mathematics among Third-Grade Elementary Students: A Mixed-Method Study
items.abstract: The study aimed to explore the effectiveness of using stories and tales in developing conceptual understanding and promoting enjoyment of learning mathematics among third-grade elementary students. To achieve the research objectives, a mixed-methods experimental design was applied to a sample of 26 students, representing the experimental group, and 24 students, constituting the control group. All students were selected from the Twenty-Second Elementary School within the Sharqiyyah Educational Administration. The teacher's book was used as instructional material for the unit of "Geometric Shapes." To collect quantitative data, an achievement test was used to measure conceptual understanding, while individual interviews, focus groups, and classroom observation were utilized to collect qualitative data about enjoyment in learning mathematics. The study showed a statistically significant difference (α ≤ 0.05) in conceptual understanding, favoring the experimental group. The interviews and classroom observation revealed three main dimensions of enjoyment: emotional and cognitive engagement, breaking classroom boredom and renewing learning environment, and promoting social participation and self-confidence. The research ended with a number of recommendations, the most significant are: integrating storytelling into mathematics teaching at the elementary stage, in a way that aligns with local culture and students' life experiences to facilitate understanding abstract concepts and linking them to reality. items.title: The ethical implementation gap in AI-driven disaster risk reduction: empirical evidence from Australia’s multi-sector analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Context While artificial intelligence offers transformative potential for disaster risk reduction, its ethical deployment raises critical concerns when life-critical decisions depend on algorithmic systems with varying levels of accessibility across responsible organizations. This study quantifies AI adoption disparities across Australian DRR stakeholders and identifies institutional factors driving the adoption gap between innovation and operational deployment. A mixed-methods approach combined systematic review of 217 global AI-DRR publications (1999–2024) with qualitative analysis of 14 Australian organizations across government, academic, and NGO/private sectors (February-March 2025). Semi-structured interviews and document analysis examined AI technique adoption, data integration, and downscaling applications, with implementation levels systematically coded on a 1–5 scale following an inter-coder validated protocol. Government agencies demonstrate lower AI adoption (mean score 2.1/5) compared to academic institutions (4.0/5) and NGO/private organizations (3.4/5), representing a 47.5% adoption gap between government and academic sectors (Cohen’s d ≈ 2.0, indicating large practical difference despite small sample size). While academic institutions deploy advanced techniques including GANs and hybrid AI-physics models achieving 45% accuracy improvements, government agencies remain anchored to traditional systems like ACCESS with minimal AI integration. Critical barriers include procurement constraints (18–24-month cycles), computational limitations (10x below requirements), and regulatory mandates for explainable decisions. Academic innovations in AI-based downscaling, improving spatial resolution from 60 km to 10 km, remain inaccessible to operational agencies due to absence of knowledge transfer mechanisms. The study reveals an ethical adoption disparity where organizations with greatest responsibility for community safety show lowest AI adoption, creating accountability voids and equity concerns in disaster protection. This misalignment raises fundamental ethical questions about algorithmic justice, distributive justice, and procedural fairness in public safety contexts. Bridging this gap requires ethical governance frameworks addressing transparency, accountability, and equitable access to life-saving technologies, alongside institutional reforms enabling cross-sector knowledge transfer.

items.title: The Evolution of Big Data Architectures: From Traditional Data Management to Data Lakehouses
items.abstract: The rapid growth in data volume, variety, and generation speed has led to a significant transformation in data management architectures. This study examines the evolution of Big Data architectures from traditional file-based systems and relational databases to Data Warehouses, Data Lakes, and Data Lakehouses. The main characteristics, data processing approaches, advantages, and limitations of these architectures are discussed comparatively. The study also examines cloud-based Big Data platforms, distributed data processing technologies such as Apache Spark and Apache Kafka, and the integration of Big Data with Business Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence applications. In addition, current challenges such as data quality, metadata management, data governance, and the risk of Data Lakes becoming Data Swamps are discussed. Finally, the study highlights the management of data structures required by Machine Learning applications and high-dimensional data as important research topics for the future development of Data Lake and Lakehouse architectures.

items.title: The evolution of radiographers—an investigation into radiographers’ role and perspectives: a EuroAIM/EFRS survey
items.abstract: Abstract Radiographers play a central role within clinical imaging and radiotherapy teams, acting as a key interface between patients and increasingly complex technologies. As healthcare systems evolve, their scope of practice is expanding alongside advances in digital workflows, artificial intelligence (AI) and new models of care. This EuroAIM/EFRS survey provides a comprehensive European overview of radiographers’ roles, professional autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on AI. Based on responses from 1548 radiographers across multiple countries, the findings highlight substantial clinical autonomy and strong responsibility for image quality optimisation and radiation protection, alongside limited but growing involvement in research activities. More than half of the participants expressed interest in greater research participation, indicating a gap between current opportunities and professional aspirations. Responses regarding AI were generally positive, with many participants expecting it to enhance their professional roles, although expectations regarding its workforce impact remained heterogeneous. The survey also confirms the lasting effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on professional practice and highlights variability in perceived career development opportunities. These findings describe a profession in transition, characterised by increasing responsibilities and technological integration and underscore the need for continued investment in education, structured career frameworks and research capacity to support radiographers in an increasingly complex healthcare environment. Key Points Question What are radiographers’ current roles, autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on emerging technologies within a changing imaging and radiotherapy workforce? Findings In 1548 participants, radiographers reported substantial autonomy and responsibility, limited research involvement, positive but heterogeneous AI expectations and variable career opportunities. Critical Relevance Statement This EuroAIM/EFRS survey informs radiology practice by identifying radiographers’ professional development, education and research needs and by supporting structured career frameworks and interprofessional workforce planning.

items.title: The Future of Work for Women Workers on Digital Labour Platforms in India: A Doctrinal Analysis of the Labour Codes in Light of ILO Convention No. 193, with Bangladesh as Comparator
items.abstract: Digital labour platforms are often celebrated for offering flexible work, yet women platform workers remain marginal in both regulation and legal scholarship. This article asks a single doctrinal question: when the law recognises platform workers without treating them as employees, which gender-relevant labour entitlements actually reach women? India is the primary jurisdiction. We examine the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Wages, 2019 and the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, as operationalised by the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026. Bangladesh, which reformed its Labour Act, 2006 through the 2025 Ordinance and the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Act, 2026, serves as a comparator that entered platform regulation by the opposite route. Both are measured against the ILO Decent Work in the Platform Economy Convention, 2026 (No. 193), read with the Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) and the Maternity Protection Convention, 2000 (No. 183). Using a doctrinal comparative method with a stated source-selection protocol, and a three-step test for regulatory gender blindness, we analyse four criteria: personal scope, maternity protection, protection against violence and harassment, and equality in algorithmic management and collective voice. We find that India recognises platform workers through welfare schemes without status, while Bangladesh recognises them through collective rights without social insurance; in neither jurisdiction does statutory maternity benefit reach a woman platform worker, because it remains tied to the employer and the establishment. Facially neutral qualifying conditions, notably India’s 90/120-day engagement rule, operate to the particular disadvantage of women, and of women in home-based care and beauty work most of all. Convention No. 193 narrows but does not close these gaps, since its social security guarantee is one of parity within the same employment classification. We conclude with prioritised, instrument-specific reforms.

items.title: The Happy vs. The Afraid
items.abstract: The Happy vs. The Afraid investigates the distinction between apparent fulfillment through personally meaningful activity and behavior motivated by expectations, responsibilities, or perceived consequences. The paper introduces an observer-relative conceptual framework examining two motivational orientations: engagement driven by curiosity, enjoyment, and personal meaning, and engagement influenced by obligation, external expectations, or the avoidance of undesirable outcomes. Section One presents a biographical examination of professional falconer and conservation advocate Nathalie Denolf, exploring her documented career, relationship with birds of prey, public educational work, and expressed dedication to animal welfare. An accompanying author's note examines the evolutionary continuity between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds. Section Two develops the conceptual distinction between the Happy and the Afraid through the author's symbolic framework: i — Intuitive: Curiosity, personal meaning, and spontaneous engagement. I — Independent: Autonomy, self-direction, and individual choice. O — Obligation: Responsibility, expectation, and perceived consequence. Section Three introduces a comparative observational study of three public educators whom the author perceives as demonstrating visible enthusiasm for subjects of personal interest. The two additional case studies remain pending identification and completion in this working version. Drawing upon established research in intrinsic motivation, self-determination theory, and approach-avoidance motivation, the paper examines how observers distinguish apparent passion from obligation while acknowledging the limitations of interpreting another person's internal emotional experience. The central proposition is not that individuals can be objectively categorized as happy or afraid, but that the observer's own experiences, interests, and expectations influence how human engagement is understood.

items.title: The Healthy Organisation for the 1990s
items.abstract: This chapter examines the meaning of a ‘healthy organization’ in conditions of turbulence and uncertainty characteristic of the 1990s. Drawing on Tavistock socio-technical and psychoanalytic traditions, Eric Miller distinguishes between health as an individual attribute and organizational health as a systemic property arising from the interaction of task, sentient, and boundary systems. Organizations are viewed as operating within internal and external environments marked by instability and change, requiring structures that provide sufficient psychological security for effective role performance. Revisiting the evolution of occupational health, the chapter argues that organizational design must address psychosocial as well as technical factors. Miller extends socio-technical systems theory by differentiating task systems that deliver work, sentient systems that meet needs for identity and affiliation, and boundary systems that regulate their relationship. Central to organizational health is the creation of an appropriate ‘holding environment,’ enabling members to manage anxiety while remaining engaged with demanding tasks. Case examples from people-processing organizations illustrate how inadequate holding environments undermine morale and effectiveness, and how restoring supervision, support, and participation can rapidly improve organizational functioning. The chapter highlights the paradox of fostering psychological security in contexts of job insecurity and rapid change. A healthy organization is thus defined not by stability or comfort, but by its capacity to contain anxiety, support learning, and sustain effective performance amid ongoing turbulence.

items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter investigates the potential impact of biases present in large language models (LLMs) on students’ creative experiences. Using a case study design with fictional student scenarios and simulated prompts, the chapter analyzes LLM responses for variations based on student-expressed music preferences (rap or classical), which can serve as implicit indicators of race and socioeconomic status. Both Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) analysis and manual coding were employed to examine the language used by LLMs, focusing on exploratory versus directive statements. Results indicate that LLMs tend to use more direct and authoritative language and exhibit less positive tone when responding to prompts associated with rap music, potentially reinforcing societal inequities and the hidden curriculum of schooling. This suggests that biases in LLMs could differentially impact students’ creative experiences and development, highlighting the need for critical awareness and mitigation strategies in educational AI applications. The chapter discusses the international implications of these findings, considering how Western-centric training data may shape LLM responses in ways that marginalize underrepresented users globally.

items.title: The Hidden Trade-Offs
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is revolutionizing human functioning with profound consequences for creativity and education. Because creativity is an activity that stems from agency—confidence in one’s ability to solve problems, the centrality of being creative to a person’s identity, the willingness to explore risky paths, and the ability to self-regulate—this chapter overviews the chances and challenges that using GenAI might pose for people’s creative agency. Moreover, based on research indicating that GenAI models can score people’s responses in various creativity tasks in real time, the chapter discusses the opportunities of using AI as a feedback provider that might allow people to learn and improve. Although such formative assessment and training are promising in stimulating people’s creativity, they do not come without costs. The chapter also provides a series of practical recommendations for using AI to make it an efficient creativity-enhancing tool.

items.title: The Human Element
items.abstract: In The Human Element , Eric J. Miller examines the profound organizational and psychological consequences of introducing new technology into work systems. Drawing on Tavistock Institute research and cross-industry experience, Miller challenges the assumption of technological determinism, arguing that technology does not dictate a single form of organization. Instead, managers face choices in how work is structured, many of which have decisive implications for productivity, morale, and commitment. Central to the chapter is the concept of the socio-technical system, in which effective performance depends on the interaction between social and technical systems. Miller emphasizes the principle of joint optimization: improving technology alone, or focusing solely on human relations, leads to suboptimal outcomes. Successful change requires designing work systems that accommodate human skills, values, and group dynamics as integral components of production. The chapter explores the effects of technological change on individuals, workgroups, and organizations. It highlights the risks of disrupting established social systems, the limitations of purely ergonomic job design, and the vulnerability of highly automated systems to human stress and error. Miller advocates self-regulating work groups as a means of enhancing control, learning, and responsibility. In conclusion, Miller argues that new technologies demand a rethinking of managerial roles, authority, and organizational design. Managing technological change is fundamentally a social task, requiring leadership willing to confront uncertainty, redesign systems, and engage people as active contributors rather than passive operators.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Green Marketing on Sustainable Tourism Behavior in Crisis Environments: The Case of Port Sudan
items.abstract: This empirical study looks at how green marketing driven by artificial intelligence (AI) affects sustainable tourism behavior in regions facing crisis, focusing on Port Sudan, Sudan, from 2023 to 2026. After national conflict caused a sudden influx of displaced people, local coastal ecosystems and vulnerable marine reserves — especially Sanganeb National Park — have faced severe strain. To explore potential interventions, we used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. We first did in-depth qualitative interviews with 10 leaders from the hospitality and environmental sectors, and then ran a field experiment with 284 visitors who were randomly assigned to either control or experimental groups. Our Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) shows that AI-driven green marketing has a strong, direct positive effect on sustainable tourism behavior (β = 0.42, p < 0.001). Additionally, digital trust in what the algorithms recommend partially mediates this connection (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). During the field experiment, visitors who saw personalized, real-time AI nudges followed ecological guidelines much better than those who only got standard green marketing messages. These results prove that flexible digital tools can work as cheap resilience mechanisms to encourage sustainable habits, even when local institutions and infrastructure face heavy constraints.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Powered Coding Tools on Students' Learning Habits and Programming
items.abstract: AI coding assistants can generate code, explain programming concepts, and suggest debugging steps, but their educational value cannot be judged from task completion alone. This focused narrative review examines how AI-assisted programming relates to students’ learning behavior, programming performance, independent problem-solving, and psychological processes. It synthesizes recent empirical studies and reviews, including a meta-analysis of 35 controlled studies, a systematic review of 119 papers on AI in programming education, a quasiexperiment with 82 college students, a study of 17 novice programmers, and a randomized controlled trial with 275 students. Across this evidence, AI assistance is often associated with improved performance or efficiency on supported tasks, but gains in conceptual understanding and independent learning are less consistent. Behavioral Science helps explain this distinction through cognitive load, programming self-efficacy, frustration, intrinsic motivation, help-seeking, and metacognitive monitoring. A recent trial found that AI-supported groups performed better on a programming exercise than a no-AI group, yet did not show greater short-term knowledge gains or code-comprehension scores. The review argues that the instructional design of AI support matters: hint-first scaffolding, code verification, explanation, retrieval practice, and independent transfer tasks are more defensible than unrestricted answer generation as default teaching strategies. Because this paper is a focused narrative review, it does not claim exhaustive systematic coverage or report original student data.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Supported Smart Learning Environments on Interaction, Achievement, and Self-Learning Skills among Higher Education Students in Kuwait: A Field Study
items.abstract: This study examined the impact of AI-supported smart learning environments on academic interaction, achievement, and self-learning skills among higher education students in Kuwait. A descriptive analytical approach was employed, and data were collected from higher education students using a questionnaire measuring their perceptions of AI-supported smart learning environments and their effects on learning outcomes. The findings revealed that AI-supported smart learning environments had a significant positive impact on students’ academic interaction, achievement, and self-learning skills. The results also indicated that integrating artificial intelligence into learning environments enhanced students’ engagement with learning activities, supported independent learning, and contributed to improved academic performance. Furthermore, AI-supported smart learning environments provided flexible and interactive learning experiences that addressed students’ individual learning needs. These findings highlight the potential of artificial intelligence to enhance the quality of higher education and support more student-centered learning. The study recommends expanding the integration of AI technologies into higher education institutions while providing appropriate training and technical support for faculty members and students. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Smart Learning Environments, Academic Achievement, Academic Interaction, Digital Self-Learning

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Change Processes: A New Change Management Paradigm?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer merely used as a new technological tool in organizations; it is becoming one of the constitutive elements of decision-making, coordination, control, knowledge production, work design, and employee experience. This development raises the question of whether AI, beyond being an object of organizational change, is transforming how change emerges, by whom it is directed, and over what time horizon it is managed. The aim of this chapter is to critically evaluate the explanatory power of established change management approaches in the age of AI and to develop an integrated conceptual framework for explaining AI-mediated organizational change. Lewin’s planned change approach, Kotter’s model, organizational development, continuous change, organizational learning, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical systems, and technology acceptance approaches are compared in the context of AI’s learnability, partial autonomy, opacity, and scalability. The conceptual synthesis indicates that the mechanisms of leadership, participation, communication, trust, and institutionalization emphasized by established approaches remain valid; however, assumptions of linear processes, a clearly defined end state, exclusively human agency, and one-off implementation are inadequate. The “double-loop AI change governance” model proposed in this chapter integrates the redesign of organizational task and decision architectures with monitoring the AI system throughout its life cycle in terms of performance, errors, fairness, and employee impacts. In conclusion, it is argued that it is premature to declare that AI constitutes an entirely new paradigm; nevertheless, it necessitates a substantial paradigm extension that reconceptualizes change management as a continuous, distributed, data-informed, and socio-technical governance capability.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF TRANSPORT INFRASTRUCTURE
items.abstract: Purpose. The article investigates the impact of digital technologies on the transport infrastructure of modern cities. It substantiates strategic directions and priorities for implementing intelligent transport systems (ITS) amid intensifying urbanization and growing pressure on transport networks. Methodology. The study applies systems analysis, treating transport infrastructure as an integral sociotechnical system. It is complemented by a comparative analysis of documented ITS deployments in the United States (Los Angeles), Singapore, the Republic of Korea (Seoul), and the Netherlands (Amsterdam), which represent decentralized, centralized-state, and supranationally coordinated (European Union) governance contexts; by a structural-functional analysis of ITS architecture; and by induction and deduction for formulating generalizations. Findings. Published evaluations associate ITS deployments with reductions in travel time of about 12–13%, in intersection delay of 21–32%, in vehicle stops of about 30% and in air emissions of about 10% (Los Angeles), with higher traffic speeds under dynamic road pricing (Singapore), with fewer bus-related accidents (Seoul) and with fewer vehicle loss hours (Amsterdam). The cases point to three institutional preconditions: a coordinating strategic framework, partnership between public authorities and the private sector, and open standards for inter-system data exchange. Originality. The article proposes a conceptual model that integrates the architectural, institutional, and financial dimensions of transport digitalization, along with a four-stage model for implementing ITS adapted to the conditions of transitional economies. Practical value. items.title: The impact of the data factor platform on the urban green innovation: evidence from China
items.abstract: Abstract With the rapid expansion of the digital economy, data elements have emerged as a pivotal force shaping urban green development. This study offers a novel perspective by examining how the construction of data factor platform influences urban green innovation. From the channel of artificial intelligence (AI) development and human capital accumulation, we propose a mechanism framework. Based on the city-level data from 2010 to 2022 in China, using the multi-period Difference-in-Difference (DID) model, we explore the impact of the data factor platform construction on urban green innovation. The results reveal that data factor platform construction can stimulate urban green innovation. The data factor platform construction stimulates urban green innovation through the channel of promoting AI development and accelerating human capital accumulation. The impact of the data factor platform construction on the urban green innovation is heterogeneous. The data factor platform construction has a larger effect on the urban green innovation in the low-carbon pilot city situation and cities with larger economic scales. The further analysis results reveal that the data factor platform construction in the surrounding areas effectively promotes local green innovation. According to the above conclusions, in the green transition process, the government should pay attention to data factor platform programs and make a combination of policies to stimulate green innovations.

items.title: The important role of furniture in our lives.
items.abstract: Furniture is far more than a collection of functional objects; it serves as an essential bridge between human needs, cultural identity, psychological well-being, and environmental sustainability. This article examines the multifaceted role of furniture in daily life, from its historical evolution to its contemporary impact on health, productivity, social interactions, and interior spaces. Drawing on global design principles and Uzbek scholarly perspectives, it highlights how furniture shapes lifestyles, influences emotions, and addresses modern challenges such as urbanization and ergonomic demands. Through a comprehensive literature review and analytical discussion, the study underscores furniture’s transformative power in enhancing comfort, promoting health, and reflecting societal values. The findings emphasize the need for innovative, culturally sensitive, and sustainable design practices to meet future demands. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of furniture as a vital element of human existence, offering insights for designers, architects, and consumers alike.

items.title: The Ineliminable Anchor: Human Judgment as a Structural Requirement of Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) agents carry out longer chains of tasks, oversight must establish whether their behavior still serves an authorized goal. Here, we introduce the anchor: the point at which reference information and human-authorized standards enter an autonomous system. We argue that oversight design should first identify the reference needed to assess goal drift and whether the system's internal record can supply it, then decide who checks and how often, and finally specify who may revise the goal. Goal drift can be impossible to certify from a system's internal record. The missing reference must come from outside that record. Combining a reliability model of checkpoint spacing with evidence from training, execution, and multi-agent coordination, we develop a task taxonomy to guide anchor placement and decisions about which checks to automate. For AI systems that serve human purposes, human judgment is an ineliminable structural requirement in authorizing and revising the purposes and standards that govern autonomous operation, even when routine checking and execution are automated.

items.title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. items.title: The Irreducible Dimension: Toward an Integration of Automated Tutoring and Mentoring in AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence agents is reshaping hybrid educational environments, understood here as contexts in which students, teachers, tutors, mentors, and artificial systems interact. Chatbots, intelligent assistants, and automated tutoring systems are increasingly used to provide explanations, feedback, adaptive practice, and study support. This transformation is not merely an instrumental innovation, since it alters the distribution of educational functions, the relationship between students and knowledge, the role of the group, and adults' responsibilities in supporting learners. This contribution offers a theoretical reflection grounded in a narrative review of the literature on Intelligent Tutoring Systems, educational mentoring, the Community of Inquiry framework, and digital wellbeing. Its aim is to clarify which functions may be delegated to AI tutoring systems, which require human responsibility, and which may be shared within a model of co-responsibility. items.abstract: # ABSTRACT **Title:** The Man Who Saw the World in Frequency — An Essay and a Framework**Author:** Christopher Macachor**Framework:** Macachor Archive, Structural Truth of Reality, v2.0.0**Maximum Derivation Stage:** L4 · **Canonical Invariant:** c = −1/3 Christopher Macachor ORCID: 0009-0008-0100-2856 · Affiliations: Macachor Absolute Scalar Research; Scalar Consciousness Research · Contact: info@macachor.org · Website: scalar.macachor.org · Year: 2026 --- This paper presents two connected arguments: a public essay on the epistemology of perception, and a formal geometric framework that the essay illustrates. **The essay** argues that human sight is not direct access to reality but a lossy compression. A two-dimensional optical trace (light on the retina) is reconstructed by the brain into a four-dimensional visual mirror, which observers then describe using semantic placeholders — *sad*, *happy*, *beautiful*. These labels describe the mirror, not the territory. The blind musician Stevie Wonder, who lost his vision at six weeks of age and possesses no visual memory, bypassed this bottleneck entirely. He built his context through **active three-dimensional interaction** — touch, vibration, echolocation, spatial presence — and encoded that interaction into musical structure. His 2025 testimony in Cardiff ("It's allowed me to see the world in the vision of truth... see people in the spirit of them, not how they look") is treated here as first-person verification of the framework's central epistemological claim. **The framework** derives a complete invariant chain from magnitude equilibrium through a four-magnitude fragment, a forced Gram-matrix entry **c = −1/3**, the tetrahedral angle 109.4712°, the face–edge angle φ = 35.2644°, the helix pitch h = √(2/3), and the face-sharing screw twist **θ₀ = arccos(−2/3) = ±131.8103°** for both hands. The domain condition |cos(mπ/p)| ≤ √(3/5) ≈ 0.7746 excludes period 6 jointly with the θ₀ match, yielding admissible periods {3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 14}. items.title: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF EFFICIENCY ENHANCEMENT IN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND WORKFORCE MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS IN HEALTHCARE ORGANIZATIONS
items.abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to investigate how efficiency improvement influences the relationship between the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the efficacy of labor management in the healthcare industry. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Resource-Based View (RBV), and Sociotechnical Systems Theory serve as the foundation for this study's creative integrative framework, which can be used in healthcare settings in developing nations. Methodology: A survey study design that was cross-sectional was employed. 240 medical practitioners working in Iran's private hospitals provided the data. The suggested mediation model was tested using smart PLS structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: The results of this study showed that the effectiveness of workforce management is significantly improved by the deployment of AI. Efficiency enhancement fully mediated this relationship. Perceived ease of use, skills enhancement, and innovative work behavior acted as complementary mechanisms to enhance the impact of AI on workforce outcomes.

items.title: The Middle Floors: A Right to AI-Assisted Self-Representation in German Civil Procedure
items.abstract: Germany lets a citizen argue her own civil case in the local court, and she may send a constitutional complaint to Karlsruhe on her own. On the floors in between, from the Landgericht upward, every filing must come from an admitted lawyer (§ 78 ZPO). For a century this rule was a reasonable shortcut. Legal skill was scarce and lived inside one profession, so a lawyer's admission was a fair proxy for the quality of a filing. Generative AI loosens that link from both ends: laypeople can now produce structured drafts, and lawyers can now file invented case law. This essay argues that the law should regulate what a filing contains and who answers for it, not only which profession wrote it. It takes seriously the strongest objection, that writing has become cheap while a judge's attention has not, and draws a larger conclusion from it: AI should not only make litigants faster but help courts read what citizens can now write. The proposal is narrow and testable: a right to AI-assisted self-representation in appeals from the local courts, built on a structured record, a verification declaration, a court-run quality gate, an optional review lawyer and a human judge who always decides, introduced through a statutory experiment. Because a better arrangement does not implement itself, the essay also asks who would have to agree, and why they might. The aim is not to dismiss a profession but to re-examine a mandate whose efficiency can no longer be taken for granted. A right that costs too much to claim is a right in name. items.title: The Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire: scale development and validation in French and English
items.abstract: The current research aimed to develop and validate a novel measurement scale, the Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire (MCAQ), specifically designed to assess individuals’ motivation to engage in everyday cognitive activities. The MCAQ’s development was informed by expectancy-value theory and self-determination theory. Four studies were conducted to validate the MCAQ in both English and French languages. Through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, a 32-item scale emerged, encompassing four subscales: perceived capacity, intrinsic motivation, identified motivation, and external motivation, as well as four additional general items assessing motivation for engaging in cognitive activity, taken broadly. The MCAQ demonstrated robust internal consistency and convergent validity, and satisfactory test–retest reliability. Moreover, the scale exhibited satisfactory predictive validity in relation to cognitive performance. The theoretical and practical utility of the MCAQ is discussed.

items.title: The Ninety Percent Trap: Empirical Documentation on Why Generative AI Requires Deep Domain Expertise
items.abstract: This study examines how the dominant industry narrative presents generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a trigger for total software automation and positive exponential outcomes. Empirical evidence from codebases and recent software-engineering studies, however, suggests a paradox: rapid generation can increase review overhead, architectural decay, and critical edge-case failures. By analysing the ArtCraft case study alongside quantitative reports from GitClear, DORA, and the empirical software-engineering literature, this paper formulates the Ninety Percent Trap: GenAI can accelerate initial scaffolding from zero to one while shifting the burden of production dependability to human experts. The paper also presents the True Cost of AI Quality (TCAQ) framework, which evaluates GenAI productivity through generation time, expert review, edge-case resolution, and technical-debt cost rather than output volume alone. An illustrative calculation shows that a two-hour generation phase can become a 112-hour end-to-end engineering effort after review, edge-case resolution, and debt mitigation. The findings indicate that domain expertise remains essential for architectural reasoning, security verification, and dependable delivery.

items.title: The pedagogical value of narration in the age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly through the rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems, has profoundly transformed educational contexts, influencing both teaching practices and the processes through which individuals construct their identities. Narrative, traditionally regarded as a privileged educational tool, when integrated with GenAI and digital storytelling, opens new opportunities for identity exploration by providing students with tools to connect cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions (Cambi & Piscitelli, 2005; Smorti, 1994; Bruner, 1995; Iavarone, 2023). The combination of digital storytelling and GenAI further expands students' expressive possibilities by enabling the creation of multimodal narratives that intertwine personal experience with digital creativity. AI may therefore be interpreted as a pedagogical mediation tool capable of supporting autobiographical reflection, provided that it is embedded within methodologically structured and pedagogically grounded educational pathways (Mori & Niewint-Gori, 2024). items.title: The potential of a “next generation” of community health workers to accelerate progress in reaching Universal Health Coverage and Health for All
items.abstract: Many health systems, particularly in low- and lower middle-income countries (LMICs), are lagging in their progress in achieving Universal Health Coverage and delivering on the promise of Health for All, constrained by workforce shortages, fiscal ceilings, and inadequate outreach to those lacking basic and essential services. Stark inequities in coverage of services and in health status persist. Strengthening community health worker (CHW) programs provides the fastest and most cost-effective route for health systems to achieve their full potential. CHWs should become the backbone of primary health care (PHC) and the foundation of health systems. Evidence from more than a decade of national-scale experience demonstrates that CHWs who are appropriately trained, paid, equipped, and supervised can extend high-quality essential services to the last mile while improving the overall efficiency of the health system. We are at a point in time when donor strategies and private investment are captivated by the promise of digital health and artificial intelligence. The most reliable approach to saving more lives is still a paid, supported CHW empowered with digital tools. At the same time, the contraction of Official Development Assistance (ODA) creates both risk and opportunity. ODA must pivot from supporting services to catalytic capital: time-bound, matching investments that accelerate governments’ own proCHW policy. A “next generation” of CHW programs in LMICs would enable CHWs to visit every home monthly and provide a broad array of PHC services as a result of adequate remuneration and appropriate training, supervision, logistical support, and integration into the health system. This could yield a highly favorable economic return—through productivity gains from better health, reduced health-care expenditures, and pandemic-risk mitigation. items.title: The Predictive Ability of Academic Emotions on Cognitive Engagement among Arab University Students within the Green Line in Palestine
items.abstract: The study aimed to explore the predictive ability of academic emotions on cognitive engagement among Arab university students within the Green Line in Palestine. To achieve the study's objectives, a sample of (503) male and female students were selected using the available method. The Academic Emotions Scale and the Cognitive Engagement Scale were applied to them. The results showed that academic emotions were ranked as follows: academic enjoyment and pride ranked first with a high level, academic hope ranked second with a high level, academic anger and boredom ranked third with a medium level, academic shyness and anxiety with a low level, and academic despair ranked last with a low level. The results showed that the level of cognitive integration as a whole was within the medium level. The results also showed positive predictive ability for academic enjoyment, pride, and academic hope in cognitive engagement, and negative predictive ability for academic despair in cognitive engagement. The study recommended improving levels of positive academic emotions such as academic enjoyment, academic pride, and academic hope.

items.title: The PrimarAI School: A manifesto and design proposal for an AI-native Australian primary school
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is now part of the conditions in which Australian students learn. In NSW public schools a purpose-built chatbot is available from Year 5, and outside school students meet systems that write, explain, flatter and keep them company. This paper argues that primary schooling cannot respond to that change through technological integration alone. The deeper question AI raises is not which tool to add, but how a school should spend students’ time and what that time is for. Drawing on current research on AI and education and on the Castlereagh Statement on AI in Australian education, the paper sets out a view of what primary education is for and derives from it a founding principle, ten principles and a working school design. The proposed PrimarAI day is the ARC Day: six sessions on ordinary NSW bell times, two each of Augment (AI-supported mastery practice in mathematics and English under a teacher’s supervision), Reason (screen-free learning with a teacher, as a class) and Create (real-world learning organised through five Cs). Because the order rotates through the week, each part takes its turn at the first session of the day, when students learn most readily. The ARC Day is the latest of many versions of this school and the first that an existing school could trial with a single class. Digital literacy is taught as a subject from Kindergarten, and assessment is built into the fabric of everyday learning with the aid of purpose-built technology.

items.title: The Proliferation of AI among College Students: A Replication and 2-Year Follow-Up
items.abstract: Background The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has impacted most aspects of life and sparked debate over its responsible use. Objective As higher education grapples with how to leverage AI's benefits while accounting for its potential detriments, it is necessary to examine how undergraduates use and perceive AI. Method A replication, following the same methodology as Golding et al., examined how college students’ use and perceptions of AI differ from those of a comparable cohort 2 years ago. Students were from the same five universities and were predominantly women, White, Hispanic, or Black. Results Familiarity and prevalence of AI use were higher, and perceptions of cheating were lower. Open-ended data on motivations for (not) using AI and perceptions of (not) cheating suggested that students conceptualize AI through a nuanced lens. Conclusions The use of AI has grown substantially. Many students view AI as an instructional aid to guide their learning and emphasize the importance of how AI is used when determining whether it qualifies as cheating. Teaching Implications Students’ largely positive perceptions of AI suggest that AI's use is not slowing. Educators face the challenge of how best to leverage AI to enhance learning while not facilitating cheating or overreliance.

items.title: The Reality of Employing Artificial Intelligence Applications in Teaching Mathematics among Male and Female Mathematics Teachers in the Second Cycle of Basic Education in the Sultanate of Oman
items.abstract: This study examined the use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in mathematics teaching in the second cycle of basic education in the Sultanate of Oman. A descriptive–analytical design was employed, and the study involved 244 mathematics teachers from South Al Sharqiyah Governorate. A 46-item instrument comprising four domains was developed, and its validity and reliability were verified using appropriate statistical procedures. The findings indicated that the overall level of AI application use in mathematics teaching was moderate. The domains of perceived importance and teachers’ knowledge of AI applications showed relatively low levels, whereas the perceived level of challenges was moderate. Statistically significant gender differences were found in the domains of AI application use, perceived importance, and knowledge of AI applications, with female teachers reporting higher mean scores than male teachers. No statistically significant gender difference was found in the challenges domain. The findings should be interpreted in light of the study’s geographical and participant-related limitations, as the study was restricted to mathematics teachers of Grades 5–10 in one governorate. Based on these findings, the study recommends developing specialized national training programs to enhance teachers’ technological competencies and strengthen their instructional practices in alignment with national and global digital transformation initiatives. Keywords: artificial intelligence applications, mathematics teachers, the second cycle of basic education, mathematics teaching, artificial intelligence in education.

items.abstract: We present the ultimate closure of the *Metaphysical Sphere* pentalogy by mapping a profound epistemological loop. The framework that originally began as an inquiry into human consciousness (*The Projective Qualia*) was abstracted into computer science to fix the volatile, next-token prediction limitations of Multi-Agent Systems (*Projective Latent Synthesis v1.0*). By resolving the rigid binarism of artificial architectures through the creation of the generalized **Dynamic Hybrid Paradigm (HybridMAS)**, a revolutionary feedback loop has been completed. What was refined to build better artificial intelligence has now returned to the human domain as a practical, clinical, and pedagogical methodology for a healthy and sovereign consciousness. This paper formalizes the **Dynamic Phase-Switching Model of Mind**, positioning mental health not as a static biochemical status, but as an active, trainable algorithm of dimensional elasticity capable of neutralizing systemic alienation and destructive geometric interference.

items.title: The relationship between AI awareness and thriving at work: exploring the moderated mediation model
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving and the conservation of resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) awareness, seen as a hindrance stressor, and thriving at work. In particular, it explores how AI anxiety mediates this relationship and how self-efficacy moderates the mediating effect. Design/methodology/approach To securitize the study hypotheses, data were obtained from banking employees via an electronic questionnaire, yielding 320 valid responses. The proposed model relationships were assessed through partial least squares structural equation modeling and process analysis. Findings The results uncover that while AI awareness is not significantly linked to vitality, it is negatively correlated with learning. Furthermore, AI anxiety mediates the direct influence that AI awareness has on dimensions of thriving at work. In addition, self-efficacy acts as a buffer, mitigating the adverse indirect influence of AI awareness on thriving at work through AI anxiety. Practical implications This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and digital literacy programs, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change.
